fact_en:
Why does okoy get so crispy?

This shrimp-and-vegetable fritter is cooked in very hot oil, which dries the outside and makes it super crispy!
fact_bis:
Nganong nagiging kuyamis ang okoy?

Kini nga prito nga hipon ug utanon giluto sa init kaayo nga mantika, nga magpauga sa gawas aron mahimong kuyamis!

findings.note: EN: "Why does okoy get so crispy? ... cooked in very hot oil, which dries the outside and makes it super crispy!" BIS: "Nganong nagiging kuyamis ang okoy? ... giluto sa init kaayo nga mantika, nga magpauga sa gawas aron mahimong kuyamis!" Cebuano 'kuyamis' is a sweet soft-meat coconut variety (the Kuyamis festival name), not crispy; crispy is malutong / tagiktik / lutong. The card's whole point is the outcome 'crispy' and it is never named correctly anywhere on the card, in the question or the answer, so a Cebuano-only child is told hot oil dries the okoy until it becomes a coconut-ish thing. Corroboration: 'kuyamis' occurs exactly once in the whole corpus (this card), while every other crispy card uses malutong / tagiktik / lutong / crispy (ffct-17817, ffct-17819, ffct-18346, ffct-18262, ffct-21471). The same Cebuano line also slips into Tagalog ('nagiging'), which is a sign this row was translated loosely. Medium-low confidence: the mechanism (very hot oil dries the surface) does survive, so the child still gets the causal fact, and a rare regional sense of kuyamis would make this a PASS.

fact_en: Air isn't just one thing! It is actually a mixture of many different gases mixed together, not just a single substance.
fact_bis: Ang hangin dili lang usa ka butang! Kini usa ka sagol o mixture sa daghang lain-laing gas, dili lang usa ka substansya.

findings.note: title_bis "Hangin Halo Daghan Gas" for "Air Is a Mixture". In Cebuano *halo* is the monitor lizard (bayawak) — mixture is *sagol*, which is exactly what this card's own body uses ("usa ka sagol o mixture"). The headline a child sees therefore reads "air monitor-lizard many gas" and never says the air is a mixture. Same Tagalog-false-friend class as langgam/gamot. Corpus check: bodies use *halo* for the lizard (ffct-00855, ffct-06130) and *sagol* for mixture (221 bodies), while ~56 TITLES use *halo* for mixture — a title-side artifact, not dialect.

fact_en: Talc is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale, with a hardness of just 1!
fact_bis: Ang talc mao ang labing humok nga mineral sa Mohs scale, nga adunay hardness nga 1 lang!

findings.note: title_bis "Talc nga Kinamumutan" — kinamumut-an means "most beloved/dearest" in Cebuano, not "softest" (kinahumokan / labing humok). The headline a child sees no longer states the property the card is about (title_en = "Talc, Softest Mineral"); it reads as "Talc the Beloved". Body still says "labing humok", so it is partly recoverable, but the title itself names a different property.

fact_en: The Mohs scale measures how hard it is to scratch a mineral!
fact_bis: Ang Mohs scale nagasukod kon unsa kalisod kalmuton ang usa ka mineral!

findings.note: title_bis "Mohs sa Kusog" = "Mohs of strength/force". Kusog is strength, loudness or speed in Cebuano; Mohs measures hardness / scratch resistance (katig-a, kagahi — this batch uses "kinatig-a" correctly in ffct-19046). The headline mislabels what the scale measures; the body ("kon unsa kalisod kalmuton") is correct.

fact_en:
What is the absolute softest mineral on Earth?

Talc is the softest mineral, and it has a Mohs hardness of just 1!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang pinakahumok nga mineral sa tibuok kalibutan?

Ang talc mao ang pinakahumok nga mineral, naay Mohs hardness nga 1!

findings.note: Same defect as ffct-19045: title_bis "Talc sa Kinamumutan" for title_en "Talc, Absolute Softest". Kinamumut-an = beloved/dearest, never "softest" (pinakahumok). Repeated across two cards, so it looks systematic rather than a one-off typo.

fact_en: The meter is the perfect unit for measuring length or distance! We use it every day.
fact_bis: Ang metro mao ang husto nga sukod sa gitas-on o gilay-on! Gigamit nato kini adlaw-adlaw.

findings.note: title_en "Meters Measure Length" -> title_bis "Metro sa Giladmon". Giladmon is DEPTH in Cebuano (corpus uses it that way 54 times: ocean depth, abyssal zone depth, stereo-vision depth), not length (gitas-on). The title tells a title-scanning child the meter is the unit for depth, a different quantity from the card's lesson. Confidence low-medium: the body correctly says "sukod sa gitas-on o gilay-on", so the defect is title-only.

fact_en: Helium (He) is the second lightest element! Because it is so light, helium balloons float high up in the sky.
fact_bis: Ang helium (He) maoy ikaduhang kinagaanan nga elemento! Tungod kay gaan kaayo kini, molutaw ang mga helium balloon sa kahanginan.

findings.note: title_bis "Helium Ikatulo Balloon" says helium is the THIRD (ikatulo) lightest; English title is "Helium Second Lightest" and the body correctly says "ikaduhang kinagaanan". The headline a child sees states a false ordinal and contradicts the body, so the card asserts two different numbers with no way to tell which is right.

fact_en:
Why do unripe Guimaras mangoes turn yellow and sweet?

Chemical changes happen as they ripen! These changes convert starches into simpler sugars.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga mo-yellow ug mo-tam-is ang mga mangga sa Guimaras kung mamala?

Adunay kemikal nga pag-usab kung mamala! Nag-convert kini sa starch ngadto sa simple nga asukal.

findings.note: Body uses 'kung mamala' (when they DRY UP) twice for EN 'as they ripen' (Cebuano: mahinog), making drying the stated cause of yellowing/sweetening and of the chemical change. Partial mitigation: title_bis 'Paghinog sa Mangga Guimaras' is correct, but the causal sentence in the body is still wrong. Lower confidence.

fact_en: Pure water is a poor electrical conductor, but dissolved impurities like sweat make it dangerous around electricity!
fact_bis: Ang limpyo nga tubig poor electrical conductor, pero kung naa’y natunaw nga impurities sama sa singot, mahimong delikado kini sa kuryente!

findings.note: title_bis 'Tubig Laway Kuryente' for EN 'Salty Water Conducts Electricity' — laway = SALIVA, not salty (parat/maalat). The body only mentions singot (sweat) and never salt, so the headline names a different substance and the card never corrects it.

fact_en: When you add heat to solid butter, its molecules get enough energy to break their rigid structure and flow as a liquid!
fact_bis: Kung pasabugan ang solid butter, ang molecules makakuha ug igo nga enerhiya aron mabungkag ang hugot nga structure ug mo-flow isip liquid!

findings.note: Cebuano replaces "add heat" with "pasabugan" (to be blown up / scattered — from sabog/pasabog, nothing to do with heat): "Kung pasabugan ang solid butter, ang molecules makakuha ug igo nga enerhiya...". Heat, the whole cause of melting, never appears anywhere on the card (title is only "Natunaw nga Mantekilya"), so a child reading only the Cebuano learns butter melts when it is exploded/sprinkled, not when heated, and cannot answer what makes butter melt. "pasabugan" occurs nowhere else in the sweep, so it is an isolated mistranslation, not a regional usage.

fact_en: Did you know water expands when it freezes into solid ice? This growing ice can actually burst closed glass bottles left inside your freezer!
fact_bis: Mogawas ang tubig kung mag-freeze kini ug mahimong solid ice! Maong makabuak ang mga siradong glass bottle nga gibutang sulod sa freezer.

findings.note: "water expands when it freezes" became "Mogawas ang tubig kung mag-freeze kini" = the water COMES OUT/escapes when it freezes — a different and physically false mechanism, and it is the emphasised phrase (emph_bis: ["Mogawas"]). It also contradicts the very next clause about SEALED bottles bursting (nothing can come out of a closed bottle). The title "Paglapad sa Yelo" is the only hint of expansion; the body sentence the child actually reads states the wrong cause. Sibling cards get this right (ffct-19920 "Mo-expand kini", ffct-19946 "Mo-expand ang nag-freeze nga tubig"), so this is a one-off defect.

fact_en:
How much weight can one cubic meter of helium gas lift?

Helium gas is lighter than air, allowing one cubic meter to lift roughly one kilogram of weight!
fact_bis:
Pila ka kilo ang kayang i-lift sa usa ka cubic meter sa helium gas?

Mas gaan kaysa hangin ang helium gas, mao nga usa ka cubic meter makapabug-at og mga usa ka kilo!

findings.note: "lift" is reversed to "make heavy" in both the title and the answer: title_bis "Helium nga Magbug-at Kilo" (helium that weighs/makes a kilo heavy) and "usa ka cubic meter makapabug-at og mga usa ka kilo" — bug-at = heavy; the Cebuano for lifting is (mak)aalsa. As written the headline tells a child helium is heavy, and the answer says a cubic metre ADDS about a kilo of weight, directly contradicting the buoyancy fact the card teaches (and "mas gaan kaysa hangin" in the same sentence). Only the question stem's English loanword "i-lift" carries the right direction.
